title: Melania Trump Calls for ‘Peace’ When Asked About Children in Gaza and Israel at Amazon Series Premiere
description: Amazon Prime Video’s “Melania: The Series” offers a peek into the often-reclusive first lady’s personal life and role inside the White House, inclu
body:
Amazon Prime Video’s “Melania: The Series” offers a peek into the often-reclusive first lady’s personal life and role inside the White House, including her efforts to provide children in foster care with educational and career opportunities.

	But as the first lady seeks a more public-facing role in international peacemaking efforts, most recently taking credit for brokering a ceasefire in Ukraine, how often does she think about the children in Gaza, Israel and other parts of the world affected by conflict?
	

	When posed the question at the New York premiere of her new two-part Amazon series, the first lady told Variety: “I want peace all around the world. That’s very important to me. We should all live in harmony and peace.”

	“I hope we can,” she added, before vaguely suggesting how that peace might be achieved: “To get together.”

	The first lady’s call for peace comes at a pivotal moment in President Donald Trump’s presidency, one where he attempts to recast himself as a global peacemaker after a bruising midterm defeat. (In the wake of the “blue wave,” Vice President JD Vance identified “end[ing] the war” and “chang[ing] our relationship to Israel” as two of the “top four causes” he and his most trusted pollsters believe could win back Republican voters who flipped their votes.)

	Efforts “to get together” were underway just hours before the Prime Video series premiere, as Presidents Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin convened for a historic trilateral summit in China. The meeting culminated in a joint declaration emphasizing peace, commitments to the United Nations and a reaffirmation that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”
	

	While Trump celebrated the meeting as a historic breakthrough (fittingly rating his trip a “12” out of 10), some foreign policy analysts argued that the summit was more spectacle than substance and raised concerns over legitimizing Putin without securing concessions on Ukraine. The joint declaration also did not directly address the ongoing conflicts in Gaza or Iran.

	The two-part docuseries is the second project released under Amazon’s $40 million licensing agreement for the Brett Ratner-directed “Melania” documentary, which debuted in January. Producer Marc Beckman oversaw the bidding war for what he calls “the biggest documentary in history.” (While the film exceeded box office expectations, its $16.6 million worldwide gross falls far short of the all-time documentary record. To put it in perspective, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything” earned more in its second weekend playing in U.S. theaters alone than “Melania” did during its entire worldwide run.)

	“I went to multiple entities, from Amazon to Netflix to Hulu to Paramount, and all of them were interested in picking up the film,” Beckman said. “I can tell you point-blank, Amazon’s team was honestly the best in Hollywood. They understood how important it was to get this story out. It’s a piece of history. It’s never been told before, and we were really impressed with the leadership at Amazon. Really great people.”

	Did Jeff Bezos participate? “No, he never was involved,” Beckman claimed. “He wasn’t involved in the negotiation, and he wasn’t involved in anything else.” (Democratic lawmakers, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have accused Bezos’ company of “bribery in plain sight,” alleging that Amazon vastly overpaid for the rights and outbid its rivals by a wide margin to curry favor with the Trump administration. Bezos defended the purchase as “a very wise business decision.”

	“Melania: The Series” is now streaming on Prime Video.

schema.headline: Melania Trump Calls for ‘Peace’ When Asked About Children in Gaza and Israel at Amazon Series Premiere

title: How to Get Started on Making a Difference as Tax Rules for Charitable Giving Change
description: Rick Baker is a wealth management expert by profession, advising many of Hollywood’s A-list on managing the money and portfolios for the long term
body:
Rick Baker is a wealth management expert by profession, advising many of Hollywood’s A-list on managing the money and portfolios for the long term in a volatile industry. 


	For Baker himself, the concept of wealth management means giving some of it away through a scholarship program that he launched more than 10 years ago in his hometown in rural Alabama. On the latest episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast, as we ease into the winter holidays, Baker offers an inspirational story of how those with means can get started making a difference in the lives of others. And Sean Weissbart, a tax expert and partner at Blank Rome in New York, explains some significant changes to charitable giving federal tax rules that take effect for 2026.

	LISTEN to the full “Strictly Business” podcast here

	Baker’s own life has been a fist-pumping story of a person from humble means seizing the opportunity through education after he received a scholarship to Alabama’s Auburn University. That set him on a path to building a tony wealth management practice in Beverly Hills over the past 35 years and counting. Baker has never forgotten the hard times he experienced growing up on a small farm in Crossville, Ala.

	“I grew up in rural Alabama with two parents who were Depression kids. My dad could not read or write,” says Baker, who is today a managing director and wealth management advisor and portfolio manager with Merrill / Bank of America.

	“I was fortunate enough to get an academic scholarship to Auburn University, and then later I attended the Wharton Business School. During that path, I learned firsthand how important education was. And so I decided to go back and start giving back in my hometown of Crossville, Alabama. A very, very rural community, about 3,000 in population. It has one red light that’s actually not even a red light. It’s a blinking yellow light. And I go back and I try to do things that will change that community and make it better and just pay it forward,” he says.


	The foundation issues scholarships for secondary education tuition. It also has a mechanism to support local youth for food, housing and transportation costs that can stand in the way of the student attending school. Baker can’t hide his emotion in explaining what it means to be able to help remove even small obstacles to achievement for underprivileged kids.


	“I remember what it was like in rural Alabama and not having anything. I remember what it was like. And I never forget that because there’s such a thin line between being mega rich and mega, mega successful and not having anything — being the guy that’s struggling from paycheck to paycheck. It’s a thin line,” Baker says. “And we just have to remember that if we are fortunate enough to be able to do something for others, we need to do that because it could easily be taken away.”
	

	Weissbart, in a separate conversation, weighs in with perspective on the new charitable giing tax rules for 2026 and beyond that were enshrined by Congress in last year’s so-called Big Beautiful Bill. 

	“There are a whole new set of rules that were enacted in 2026 that changed the landscape for how one goes about getting an income tax deduction for charitable giving,” Weissbart says.

	Among them is a stipulation that the first half-percent of an individual’s adjusted gross income “is not eligible to be deducted as a charitable deduction,” he says. Translation, per Weissbart: A half-percent of a person’s adjusted gross income is taken off the top of any tax deduction for a charitable donation. For a person making $500,000 a year, one-half percent is $2,500. Therefore, if the person makes $10,000 in charitable donations, only $7,500 qualifies for a write-off.

	After a roller-coaster week on Wall Street that saw the Anthropic IPO generate enormous wealth and a bumper crump of multimillionaires (at least on paper), Weissbart notes that stock gifts to charity can be a great offset to support a worthy cause and avoid high capital gains taxes. 
	

	“We’re talking about a very, very significant savings that actually mitigates the loss of that asset on your balance sheet,” he says.

	(Pictured: Wealth manager Rick Baker with students at his hometown high school in Crossville, Ala.)

schema.headline: How to Get Started on Making a Difference as Tax Rules for Charitable Giving Change

title: Hello Sunshine’s Lauren Neustadter to Leave Reese Witherspoon’s Company at End of Year
description: Lauren Neustadter, president of film and television at Reese Witherspoon‘s Hello Sunshine, is set to step down from the company at the end of the y
body:
Lauren Neustadter, president of film and television at Reese Witherspoon‘s Hello Sunshine, is set to step down from the company at the end of the year, the collaborators announced on Friday. Her exit comes after Hello Sunshine let go of about 50% of its staff last month after Witherspoon and Mediawan partnered to buy the company back from Candle Media. 

	“Lauren’s taste, passion and leadership have been integral to Hello Sunshine’s film and television success,” Witherspoon said in a statement. “I’m so proud of what we accomplished together and grateful for her partnership and the lasting foundation she built around telling powerful, complex female-driven stories that resonate.”
	

	Neustadter added in a statement, “Building Hello Sunshine alongside Reese and our incredible team has been the privilege of a lifetime. I’m deeply proud of all the shows and movies we’ve made, the doors we’ve opened for new voices, and the ways we have put women in the spotlight both in front of and behind the camera. I am grateful for every moment of it, and I will always be cheering for Hello Sunshine.”

	Neustadter joined the company in 2017, and has served as executive producer on series including “The Morning Show,” “Big Little Lies,” “Little Fires Everywhere” and “The Last Thing He Told Me.” She oversaw adaptations of books from Reese’s Book Club including “Tiny Beautiful Things” and “Daisy Jones & the Six.” She also worked on feature films including “Where the Crawdads Sing” and TriStar’s upcoming “The Nightingale.”

	Neustadter started her career as a film executive at Miramax and Twentieth Century Fox, then became an executive at FOX network, where she oversaw “Brooklyn Nine-Nine,” “The Mindy Project” and “Lethal Weapon.”
	

	Hello Sunshine plans to focus on premium film and television and Reese’s Book Club, as well as expanding into new storytelling formats and distribution models.

	The news was first reported by the Hollywood Reporter.

schema.headline: Hello Sunshine’s Lauren Neustadter to Leave Reese Witherspoon’s Company at End of Year

title: E.J. Carroll, ‘Law & Order,’ ‘GTA 5’ and ‘Blue Bloods’ Actor, Dies at 66
description:
E.J. Carroll, who appeared in projects including “The Deuce,” “Law & Order” and “Grand Theft Auto V,” died on Thursday. He was 66.

	Carroll died s
body:
E.J. Carroll, who appeared in projects including “The Deuce,” “Law & Order” and “Grand Theft Auto V,” died on Thursday. He was 66.

	Carroll died suddenly Thursday morning, his rep confirmed to Variety. No cause of death has been provided.

	Throughout his nearly 30-year career, Carroll’s credits included Darren Aronfsky’s “The Wrestler” and Robert De Niro and Kate Beckinsale’s “Everybody’s Fine,” as well as “The Cake Eaters,” “The Capers,” “The Winning Season,” “The Hungry Ghosts” and “A Fish Story.” One of the actor’s most recognizable roles was as Fat Mooney in HBO’s “The Deuce,” where his character ran a sex shop owned by Frankie Martino (James Franco).
	

	Born on May 21, 1960, Carroll made his on-screen debut in 1998 as a police officer in “Law & Order,” later returning for two episodes of “Law & Order: SVU” and an additional two in “Law & Order: Criminal Intent.” As a guest star, Carroll appeared in projects such as “The Blacklist,” “Blue Bloods,” “High Maintenance,” “Pose” and “The Punisher.” He also starred as Sheriff Victor Sickles in two episodes of Terence Winter and Martin Scorsese’s “Boardwalk Empire” in 2012 before going on to appear in an episode of “Damages,” which starred Glenn Close and Rose Byrne, that same year.

	He also voiced a character in “Grand Theft Auto V” in 2013 and played Dr. Scott in the concert version of “The Rocky Horror Show,” titled “The Rocky Horror Tribute Show.” The concert ran for one night in 2007 to raise money for cancer charities Acting for a Cure and Komen for the Cure.
	

	Prior to his death, Carroll most recently starred in “A Delicate Arrangement,” the upcoming Vivian Leigh biopic. Starring Carla Gugino as the “Gone With the Wind” actress, the film is written and produced by Jayce Bartok and directed by Nick Sandow.

schema.headline: E.J. Carroll, ‘Law & Order,’ ‘GTA 5’ and ‘Blue Bloods’ Actor, Dies at 66

title: CMA Awards See a 55% Ratings Bump in Key Adult Demo With Taylor Swift’s Return to the Show
description: The CMA Awards‘ producers knew it; they knew her. What they undoubtedly knew was that a performance by Taylor Swift would bring a ratings bonanza t
body:
The CMA Awards‘ producers knew it; they knew her. What they undoubtedly knew was that a performance by Taylor Swift would bring a ratings bonanza to the 60th annual telecast, with the only question being how big a boost. It was a substantial one, as ratings released Friday showed the 2026 show being up 26% in total viewers and an even more impressive 55% gain in the key 18-49 demo, versus the previous year’s tallies.

	With help from Swift’s performance of a “I Knew It, I Knew You”/”Our Song” medley, the CMAs had their highest overall viewership in seven years, ABC announced. The show drew 7.62 total viewers, versus 6.03 million in 2025, for that 26% increase. The 18-49 share of the audience, where the 55% growth was found, had the telecast earning a 1.01 rating, compared to a 0.65 share last year.
	

	Not every bit of that increase necessarily had to do with Swift. America has certainly been high on Ella Langley, who did at least as well as anticipated in the awards, sweeping nearly every category she was up for to win a record six CMA Awards. Her “Choosin’ Texas” song is currently enjoying its 28th week atop Billboard’s Hot 100 chart, an all-time record — although Langley chose to sing a different song on the telecast, her latest single, “Loving Life Again.” (The singer’s performance of the then-new “Choosin’ Texas” on the CMAs last year has been cited by her label as giving the hit its biggest turbo boost.)

	Also possibly a factor in viewer anticipation for the show was the promise of a Dolly Parton tribute. The show opened with host Lainey Wilson and Vince Gill dueting on “I Will Always Love You,” a scaled-down but still very well-received homage, in comparison to the all-star Parton tribute special the Country Music Association and ABC put on in October. Other stars on the show included country drawing powers like Kacey Musgraves, Miranda Lambert, Tucker Wetmore, Chris Stapleton, Megan Moroney, Luke Combs and what turned out to be a controversial hard-rock salute to Brooks & Dunn.
	

	But without a doubt, the increase would not have been in such remarkable double-digits range without Swift. A previous Variety report, “Taylor Swift’s CMA Return Helped Disney Sell More Ads,” noted that ABC even re-opened its previously closed advertising space for the three-hour telecast after Swift officially signed on with a performance.

	The superstar had announced that she would be attending the show as soon as the nominations came in, with Swift landing one for her Disney/Pixar “Toy Story 5” closing theme song. But the fact that she would be performing was not revealed until days before the show. Swift last performed on the CMA Awards telecast in 2013; she last made an appearance on the show in 2016.

	Swift made her performance an all-star affair, beginning the number with a pre-taped and highly choreographed trip through the backstage area that had her meticulously interacting with Brooks & Dunn, Lainey Wilson, Eric Church, Sugarland, Little Big Town and Brad Paisley, all of whom she has some kind of history with. Then, with a symbolic toss back and forth with Bill Anderson, the longest-serving Grand Ole Opry member, it kicked to the live performance and she took to a “Toy Story”-themed set to complete the number, with Keith Urban on ganjo, throwing in a snippet of her first country No. 1 from 20 years ago, “Our Song.”

	Later in the show, she presented a lifetime achievement award to Brooks & Dunn.

	The CMAs telecast on Wednesday evening was preceded the night before on ABC by a preview show, “Darius, Dolly and 60 Years of Celebration: Countdown to the CMAs with Robin Roberts.” That Tuesday broadcast picked up 2.99 million total viewers, getting a 0.29 rating among adults 18-49 and a 0.38 among adults 25-54.

	The CMAs marked Swift’s first public performance of “I Knew It, I Knew You,” after she’d previously sung it at the Motion Picture Academy’s governors ball and at private awards-circuit showcases. It may not be the last the public sees and hears of Swift doing it. She was just nominated this week for a Grammy for song of the year for the film theme, and is hoping to be nominated for a best song Oscar for the first time. It’s likely both Grammys producers and Oscar producers will be hoping for their own Swift mashups, although a possible nomination for the Academy Awards is still two months away.

schema.headline: CMA Awards See a 55% Ratings Bump in Key Adult Demo With Taylor Swift’s Return to the Show

title: ‘Four Minus Three’ Takes Cairo Film Festival’s Golden Pyramid, While ‘Summer Meadow’ Wins Three Awards and ‘The Day of Wrath’ Nabs Two
description: Austrian filmmaker Adrian Goiginger’s “Four Minus Three” emerged as the big winner at the 47th Cairo Intl. Film Festival, taking home three awards,
body:
Austrian filmmaker Adrian Goiginger’s “Four Minus Three” emerged as the big winner at the 47th Cairo Intl. Film Festival, taking home three awards, including the Golden Pyramid for best film, as the festival wrapped its 10-day run in the Egyptian capital on Friday.

	The Austrian-German drama, which follows a professional clown struggling to find hope after losing her family in a car accident, also earned best actress for Valerie Pachner and best supporting actor for Robert Stadlober. Franco-Moroccan filmmaker Nabil Ayouch (“Everybody Loves Touda”) headed the international competition jury.
	

	French filmmaker Rudi Rosenberg took the Silver Pyramid for best director for “Words of Love,” while Egyptian filmmaker Ashgan El-Hamus received the Bronze Pyramid special jury prize for “Al Baraneya.” Moroccan filmmaker Laïla Marrakchi and screenwriter Delphine Agut won best screenplay for “Strawberries.” The Henry Barakat Award for best artistic contribution went to cinematographer Marius Panduru and production designer Hendrik Van Kets for the Belgian-Dutch-German co-production “Heysel 85,” which revisits the deadly 1985 Heysel Stadium disaster in Brussels. The film, directed by Teodora Ana Mihai, also won the FIPRESCI critics’ prize.

	In the Horizons of Arab Cinema competition, Rania Rafei’s “The Day of Wrath: Tales from Tripoli,” a documentary tracing decades of political uprisings in Lebanon’s second-largest city, won best Arab film and the festival’s best documentary award.

	Sara Shazli’s “Your Daughter,” a personal documentary exploring the Egyptian filmmaker’s complicated relationship with her mother, producer and filmmaker Marianne Khoury, received the Horizons special jury prize.
	

	Naël Khleifi and Lisa Debauche’s “Summer Meadow,” which follows a Lebanese apprentice shepherdess living in isolation in the French Alps, collected three prizes, including the $10,000 best Arab feature film award and a shared creative achievement prize. Manal Issa also won best acting performance for the film, after previously winning the Pardo for Best Performance in Locarno’s Cineasti del Presente competition for the same role. Mohamed Zineddaine’s “Until Dawn” shared the creative achievement award.

	In the Critics’ Week section, Lorenzo Ferro and Lucas A. Vignale’s “The River Train,” an Argentine drama about a nine-year-old folk dancer who dreams of escaping his rural village for Buenos Aires, won best film. Azamat Shargyn’s “Before the Sun Rises in the West” received the special jury prize, while Ishtiyak Ahmad Zihad’s “The Blind Girl and an Elephant” earned a special mention.

	In the short film competition, Lenti Liang’s “Our Secrets” won best short film, while Pranav Bhasin’s “We Were Here” received the special jury prize. Sabrine Khoury’s “A Tenderness” earned a special mention.

	The Youssef Cherif Rizkallah Audience Award went to Egyptian director Ahmad Abdalla’s “BerleeN_,” an ensemble drama following three Arab residents of the German capital whose lives intersect over the course of a single day.

	The closing ceremony at the Cairo Opera House also saw veteran Egyptian cinematographer Said Shimi receive the Golden Pyramid Lifetime Achievement Award.

	Marking 50 years since its founding in 1976, this year’s festival presented 145 films from 64 countries, including 17 world premieres, five international premieres and 87 MENA premieres. The event drew 53,000 ticket sales, according to festival president Hussein Fahmy, up from approximately 45,000 last year.

	The program included screenings of restored Egyptian classics, the new Cairo Kids section and masterclasses with filmmakers Matteo Garrone and international competition jury president Nabil Ayouch, who were both honored with Golden Pyramid Lifetime Achievement Awards at the festival’s opening ceremony.

	The festival’s eighth Cairo Industry Days brought together filmmakers, producers and industry professionals for workshops, pitching sessions and discussions. Its 12th Cairo Film Connection featured 17 projects from 12 countries that competed for 53 awards with a combined value of $410,000, including cash grants, in-kind services and invitations to international industry platforms.

schema.headline: ‘Four Minus Three’ Takes Cairo Film Festival’s Golden Pyramid, While ‘Summer Meadow’ Wins Three Awards and ‘The Day of Wrath’ Nabs Two

title: ‘Home Alone’ Director Chris Columbus Said Minutes Before New Sequel Was Announced That Another Movie ‘Can’t Happen’ After Catherine O’Hara’s Death
description:
Chris Columbus didn’t know a new “Home Alone” was coming.

	The director of the 1990 original spoke with Variety minutes before news broke that Dis
body:
Chris Columbus didn’t know a new “Home Alone” was coming.

	The director of the 1990 original spoke with Variety minutes before news broke that Disney is developing a new installment with Macaulay Culkin. According to sources, Columbus had no knowledge that the project was in development or about to be announced. When asked about the franchise’s future, his answer was that any return faces a steep climb without Catherine O’Hara.
	

	“Catherine, as I’ve always said, is 50% of ‘Home Alone,’” Columbus says. “There’s the yin and yang of ‘Home Alone’: Catherine O’Hara and Macaulay Culkin. Without those two in the film, there is no film, because they create the emotional epicenter of that film.”

	O’Hara, who played Kevin McCallister’s mother, Kate, died Jan. 30 at 71.

	As reported Friday, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg are shaping the script with Culkin and will produce through their Point Grey banner. The project is in early development at Disney, and plot details and casting remain under wraps. According to Deadline, the film grew out of a pitch Culkin made to Disney film chief David Greenbaum, told from the point of view of an older Kevin as a father.

	When Variety followed up after the announcement, Columbus declined to comment further.

	Columbus, who is set to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in December, was particularly warm about his former star’s return to the role in a McDonald’s holiday commercial released Nov. 17. “I love Macaulay’s McDonald’s commercial,” he says. “Macaulay is a great actor, and I hope to work with him on something. Maybe it’ll be ‘Home Alone’-related, maybe it won’t.”
	

	He leaves the door open to a return built around the original ensemble.

	“I think you potentially could still entertain the idea of doing another ‘Home Alone’ with the cast,” Columbus explains. “Not any of these ridiculous follow-ups to the first. And I only say ridiculous because it’s weird with filmmakers. They don’t understand why that cast works so well. It’s always about the cast. It’s like ‘The Goonies.’ It’s about the cast.”

	The franchise continued without Culkin and Columbus in “Home Alone 3” (1997), “Home Alone 4” (2002), “Home Alone: The Holiday Heist” (2012) and Disney+’s “Home Sweet Home Alone” (2021).

	But Columbus says O’Hara’s death has changed what a reunion could be. “It was really about Catherine and Macaulay, if anyone ever wanted to do a sequel,” he says, “and unfortunately that can’t happen now.”

	He also makes the case for the film’s burglars, Harry and Marv, played by Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern.

	“Let’s not downsize Harry and Marv,” Columbus says. “Daniel Stern and Joe Pesci are the ultimate comic duo for that particular film. Everyone has tried in subsequent sequels to be as funny or as interesting as Dan and Joe, and they just had a chemistry that is undefinable. So you can’t do that.”

	Columbus, who also directed 1992’s “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York,” has long been skeptical of revisiting the property. In 2020, he told Insider that Disney’s planned reboot was “a waste of time” and that “nobody got in touch with me about it.” That project became “Home Sweet Home Alone.” Last year, he told Entertainment Tonight that another “Home Alone” would be a “mistake.”

	Rogen also has a personal connection to O’Hara. She played studio executive Patty Leigh in his Apple TV comedy “The Studio,” a role she still held when she died. O’Hara also spoke at Culkin’s own Walk of Fame ceremony in December 2023.

	Columbus is next set to direct “Gremlins 3,” which is scheduled to begin shooting early next year. He executive produced Robert Eggers’ upcoming horror film “Werwulf,” which Focus Features opens Dec. 25.

schema.headline: ‘Home Alone’ Director Chris Columbus Said Minutes Before New Sequel Was Announced That Another Movie ‘Can’t Happen’ After Catherine O’Hara’s Death

title: ‘Being Heumann’ Producers Team With Marc Furmie, Rezistor Films on Cult Comic ‘Deadworld’ Film — Film News in Brief
description: “Being Heumann” producers Kevin Cleary and John W. Beach, of Gravity Squared Entertainment, are joining with Marc Furmie of Rezistor Films to adapt
body:
“Being Heumann” producers Kevin Cleary and John W. Beach, of Gravity Squared Entertainment, are joining with Marc Furmie of Rezistor Films to adapt and produce “Deadworld.”

	Furmie will direct from his own screenplay, an adaptation based on the original cult comic franchise from Caliber Entertainment. Filming begins in Australia in 2027, with casting set to be announced in the new year.


	“Deadworld” is a post-apocalyptic road movie following a group of juvenile delinquents. The ragtag band accepts a mission to deliver a scientist and a child to a distant refuge but soon discover they are the last line of defense against a horde of demons intent on opening a dimensional gate to hell.
	

	“This is a passion project for me that I have been developing with Caliber for several years now, and I am excited to work with Kevin and John to bring a very ambitious vision to life,” Furmie said. “We’ve designed an edgy and commercial epic, driven by a Gen-Z / Gen-Alpha cast, that is heavily inspired by Mad Max: Fury Road, Come and See and Seven Samurai. After years of grinding on smaller films in the US, Deadworld will allow me the opportunity to return home to Australia and work with my favorite collaborators to push the envelope on a larger canvas.”

	Designed as a launch point for a wider franchise, the film adapts the first story arc of Caliber’s long-running series, which spans more than 100 issues and 20+ graphic novels. Cleary, Beach and Furmie produce. Jason Mavraidis and Ty Linegar of Rezistor Films and Eric Reichert of Caliber executive produce.
	
	
		Thursday, Nov. 19	
	
		Josh Server, Yasmine Sahid, Tyler Gaca and Alexander Huntley Join Tubi Horror-Comedy ‘Do You Like Me?’	

	Tubi’s upcoming horror-comedy “Do You Like Me?” has cast Josh Server (“All That,” “The Neighborhood”), Yasmine Sahid (“Never Have I Spent the Winter with the Romano Brothers”), Tyler Gaca and Alexander Huntley.

	Set to release in 2027, the film follows friends-with-benefits Owen (Gaca) and Sam (Huntley) whose camping trip takes a deadly turn when they become stranded in the woods and seek shelter in a stranger’s cabin.

	The film also stars Curtis Edward Jackson, Narea Kang and Fadeke Oparinde with a screenplay by Gaca and Huntley. Alexander Haessner serves as director and director of photography. “Do You Like Me?” is a production of Bohemia Group Originals and Outshine Entertainment, with Justin Ross and Kiah Stern producing. Shawn Balentine serves as co-producer.
	
		Newton Thomas Sigel to Receive American Society of Cinematographers Lifetime Achievement Award	

	Newton Thomas Sigel will be honored with the Lifetime Achievement Award from the American Society of Cinematographers.

	Sigel photographed “Bohemian Rhapsody,” which earned him a BAFTA nomination and went on to be one of the highest-grossing music biopics ever. His work with director Bryan Singer on “The Usual Suspects” kickstarted a partnership spanning 10 films, including “Superman Returns,” “Valkyrie” and four “X-Men” titles. Other credits include “Blood and Wine,” “Fallen,” “Confessions of a Dangerous Mind,” “Leatherheads,” “The Brothers Grimm,” “Towelhead,” “Da 5 Bloods” and “Marshall.”

	“Tom Sigel has consistently elevated the art of cinematography through his bold visual storytelling and deep commitment to collaboration,” said ASC President Shelly Johnson. “His contributions span an extraordinary range of films and genres, each marked by a clarity of vision and a profound respect for the craft. This Lifetime Achievement Award celebrates not only his remarkable accomplishments, but the enduring legacy he has built within the cinematography community.”

	The award will be presented at the 41st Annual Outstanding Achievement in Cinematography Gala on March 7, 2027, which will be held at The Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills, California, and livestreamed globally. Other honorees include Robert McLachlan, Dejan Georgevich, Julianne Grosso and the Tiffen Company.
	

	McLachlan will receive the Career Achievement in Television Award, Georgevich will be presented with the President’s Award, Grosso will receive an Award of Distinction and Tiffen will be recognized with the Curtis Clark Technology Award to spotlight its creative and cultural influence on cinematography.
	
		Wednesday, Nov. 18	
	
		Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Patricia and David Keighley to be Honored at HPA Awards	

	The creative and technical team behind Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” along with Patricia and the late David Keighley, will be honored at the Hollywood Professional Association Awards on Dec. 3.

	“The Odyssey” creative team will receive the HPA Judges Award for Creativity and Innovation. The award recognizes companies and individuals who have made contributions to creative storytelling and technical innovation. It is not awarded annually but reserved for groundbreaking work.

	Producer Emma Thomas will accept the award on behalf of the team, led by Nolan and including cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema, editor Jennifer Lame, production designer Ruth De Jong, costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, composer Ludwig Göransson, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, special effects supervisor Scott R. Fisher, supervising sound editor Craig Henighan, production sound mixer Willie Burton, rerecording mixer Gary Rizzo, super supervising dialogue & ADR editor David Cutler, casting director John Papsidera, makeup designer Luisa Abel and hair designer Gloria Casny.

	Imax Chief Quality Guru Patricia Keighley and the late David Keighley will receive the HPA Legacy Award, which recognizes leaders, mentors and influencers who contribute to the industry. The award was first presented in 2019 to veteran journalist Peter Caranicas.

	For more than 50 years, the Keighleys have worked on post-production for over 500 large-format documentary and feature films. They created and oversaw the development of the next-generation Imax Film Camera used to shoot “The Odyssey.”

	The HPA Awards will be held Dec. 3 at 6 p.m. at the ASC Clubhouse in Hollywood.

	*

	‘The Eyes of Ghana’ Reaches 1 Million Views on YouTube in One Day

	Ben Proudfoot’s acclaimed documentary “The Eyes of Ghana” has reached 1 million views on IShowSpeed’s YouTube channel in a single day.
	

	The Breakwater Studios, Higher Ground and IShowSpeed production was released on YouTube on Tuesday following a livestream announcement the previous day between filmmakers Ben Proudfoot and Nana Adwoa Frimpong, Ethan Lewis from Higher Ground, Yaw Amponsah Apenteng, subject Chris Hesse, President Barack Obama and IShowSpeed.

	The documentary follows Ghanaian cameraman Chris Hesse’s mission to rescue a hidden film archive documenting the birth of African independence. It is produced by IShowSpeed under his name Darren Watkin, directed by Ben Proudfoot and executive produced by President Barack Obama and Michelle Obama.

	“Ghana and Africa mean so much to me,” IShowSpeed said in a statement. “Chris Hesse’s story matters and we’re not waiting on anybody to tell us which stories matter. We’re bringing this film to the world, for free. Chris Hesse spent his life protecting this important history. He deserves this moment. Ghana deserves this moment.”
	
		Tuesday, Nov. 17	
	
		Jane Lynch to Host AARP Movies & TV for Grownups Awards	

	Jane Lynch will host the 2027 AARP Movies & TV for Grownups Awards Jan. 9, celebrating the year’s top films, television programs and performances for audiences over 50 years old.

	“We wanted a host who could bring sharp wit, warmth and impeccable timing to this year’s celebration and Jane Lynch delivers on every front,” said Myechia Minter-Jordan, the CEO of AARP. “These awards honor the artists who are redefining what’s possible on screen at every age, and Jane is the perfect person to help us celebrate creative work that expands representation and reflects the richness of people’s lives.”

	Lynch will also announce this year’s nominees live on AARP’s Instagram and Facebook channels Monday at 9 a.m. PT, spanning categories that include best actor, actress and TV series or limited series.

	“I’m thrilled to join AARP Movies & TV for Grownups as host,” Lynch said. “The longer I’ve worked in this business, the more I’ve come to appreciate the depth, perspective and insight that experience brings to great storytelling. I’m looking forward to celebrating the artists and creators whose work has entertained us, surprised us and stayed with us long after the credits rolled.”
	

	AARP Movies & TV for Grownups Awards will be broadcast Feb. 26 at 6 p.m. PT on PBS and will stream on the “Great Performances” YouTube channel the following day.
	
		Monday, Nov. 16	

	David Alan Grier and Sarah Finn to Be Honored at Yale in Hollywood Fest

	The three-day virtual film festival Yale in Hollywood Fest will honor David Alan Grier with the Legacy Award and Sarah Finn with the Career Achievement Award.

	Grier is a Tony Award-winning actor and comedian, currently starring in NBC’s “St. Denis Medical.” He is the first recipient of the Legacy Award.

	Finn is an award-winning casting director. Previous recipients include actress Jennifer Beals, actor C.S. Lee and television creator Justin Noble.

	The festival will also spotlight Yale School of Music alumnus and filmmaker Charles Kaufmann, presenting his feature documentary “Tenacity: The Story of Edwin and Elise Harleston” alongside three of his short films.

title: ‘He Walked So I Could Run’: ‘Project Hail Mary’ Breakout James Ortiz on Andy Serkis, Becoming Rocky and the Art of Puppetry
description: The reason so many of us cried at “Project Hail Mary” has five legs, no face and a voice that belongs to James Ortiz. And he’s so damn effective.
body:
The reason so many of us cried at “Project Hail Mary” has five legs, no face and a voice that belongs to James Ortiz. And he’s so damn effective.

	In April, Variety exclusively reported that Amazon MGM would submit Ortiz for best supporting actor at the 99th Academy Awards for his performance as Rocky. We’ve written plenty of consideration stories. None has produced what that one did: TikToks, Instagram Reels and a corner of film Twitter demanding, with real passion, that someone “get this adorable rock creature nominated for an Oscar immediately,” as Mike Sawicki of the “Mike, Mike and Oscar” YouTube channel and podcast put it.
	

	The groundswell even made it to NBC’s “Today,” where Carson Daly spotlighted it.

	Months later, sitting in the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast studio, Ortiz still sounds like he’s processing all of it. “Did this actually happen?” he says with a wince. “It feels like it happened to somebody else two years ago.”

	It did happen.

	On this episode, Ortiz talks about bringing Rocky to life through his puppet artistry, from the eight weeks his team spent turning subtext into movement to the hours of reference footage that guided Framestore’s animators. He also lays out what he wants from Hollywood when it comes to recognizing and protecting puppetry work, why Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s set felt like “putting on a play in their parents’ garage” and the “Batman Forever” obsession that shaped him as a kid.

	Listen below.

	Lord and Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s novel opened in March to $80.5 million domestically, a record for Amazon MGM and went on to gross more than $680 million worldwide, the non-franchise phenomenon the theatrical business had been praying for. At its center, opposite Ryan Gosling’s Ryland Grace, sits Rocky, the Eridian engineer built by Neal Scanlan’s creature shop and performed on set by Ortiz and a team of puppeteers he assembled. He was hired to operate the character. The voice was supposed to come later, from someone more famous. At the 11th hour, it was his.
	

	Born in Albany and raised in Texas, the Puerto Rican and Italian artist trained classically at Purchase College and found puppetry when the acting jobs didn’t come. His first agent told him he wouldn’t work until he was 40. He turned 40 a couple of months before cameras rolled. Onstage, he won an Obie for “The Woodsman,” designed the puppets for Lincoln Center’s “The Skin of Our Teeth” and created Milky White, the scene-stealing cow of the 2022 Broadway revival of “Into the Woods.” “Project Hail Mary” is his first film.

	What strikes me is how plainly he describes the work as acting. He breaks down a script the way he once broke down Prospero and Oberon. The only difference, he says, is that he funnels those choices “through an external shell.” That’s why the conversation around him matters.

	We’ve had versions of this debate before, with Frank Oz’s Yoda, Andy Serkis’ Gollum and Zoe Saldaña in “Avatar.” Ortiz is eligible for both the Oscars and the Actor Awards, where SAG-AFTRA covers puppeteers. In theater, he points out, puppeteers are most often classified as crew.

	He isn’t campaigning for a trophy so much as for recognition of a craft. “The goal is to create a character that you get lost in,” he says. “But I think there’s value in talking about the folks that made that.”

	Excerpts from the episode, edited and condensed for clarity, are below.

	
		See all Academy Awards predictions	

	Variety Awards Circuit: Oscars




	

					“Project Hail Mary”
									Amazon MGM Studios
	


	
		You shot “Project Hail Mary” about two years ago. What was the wait like?	

	The way we approached making that thing, even though it was my first film ever, felt, from what I understand, quite avant-garde. In a funny way, it felt like I was doing some downtown play every day. But I left every day going, “I don’t really know what we just made.” There was such an emphasis on crafting and improvising on the take that there were so many different versions of every single second of that film. So two years of waiting was pretty brutal.

	I was so pleased and surprised when I got to see the final thing, especially when, at the 11th hour, I was told I was going to be the voice. And then the studio and the team said, “Why don’t we talk about this?” That’s a really unusual thing for suit performers and mocap and puppeteers.
	
		You originally trained as an actor. How did puppetry become your career?	

	My goal was always to be an actor. I went through this classical training program at Purchase, and it was all Shakespeare and Chekhov, all the things I’m still really passionate about. Then it’s that funny thing: What do you do with that information? How do you sell cereal? How do you do a bite and smile?

	The first agent I signed with, in my early 20s, the ink was literally still wet on the contract, said, “You know, you’re not going to work until you’re 40.” And I turned 40 a couple of months before we started shooting “Hail Mary.” Isn’t that nuts? So maybe he was right. Who cares?
	

	I was always drawn to painting and drawing and sculpting. My father was always engineering and tinkering and building things in the house. My mother is an academic, really literary and taught me about story structure. Long story short, all of those elements go directly into puppetry. I loved acting, performing, directing, engineering and fine art and it felt like I gamed the system by finding something where I didn’t have to pick one. When the acting gigs weren’t coming in, one thing accidentally led to another. I said, “Yeah, I can do that for this wacky downtown show for $200″ and it kick-started this thing.

	It’s become a way for me to play characters I would never, ever be cast as. That’s the thing I found about puppetry: It ends up being the most freeing form of acting because I don’t have to start from how you perceive me.
	
		Some people might see puppetry as a technical achievement. How do you approach it as an acting performance?	

	On any other role I’ve played, sans puppet, I would have ripped the script apart trying to figure out who this soul is. How do they think? How do they love? What are they terrified of? Then the exercise becomes how you funnel that through your human shell, physically and emotionally. The only difference with puppetry is that I’m funneling it through an external shell. I’m doing all of the homework.

	My approach, maybe because I started as an actor, whether it was creating Milky White on Broadway or “The Skin of Our Teeth” for Lincoln Center or the operas I’m doing, was always: What do we want the audience to feel? The precision will come later. This is a tool to play a character that should not be played by a person. So let’s take advantage of it. Let’s not let it be pedestrian.
	
		Rocky became an ensemble performance involving multiple puppeteers. How did that collaboration work?	

	I was originally going to play the puppet entirely by myself on set. Then we saw the scale of it and how many legs he had. We knew that from the book, but seeing the puppet, I raised my hand and said, “Guys, I do a lot of ensemble puppetry and ensemble direction in my theatrical career. I would love to bring in other local puppet artists and build a team.” Not people who are just there to hold a leg. I needed to get them inside my head so we could play this character together.

	For about eight weeks before we shot, we focused on how to use movement to express subtext. This is a character coming from a pretty traumatic 80 years alone in space. This character has never been alone before in their life. They’re a eusocial species, so they truly don’t know what it is to be solo. How does that existential pain manifest physically? That’s the delicious stuff. And I’m making it sound like we did a Bergman film. There was a lot of humor and silliness, but all of that has to come from something that feels grounded.
	
	
		How do you explain a performance that involves an entire team rather than one actor?	

	This might sound a little crazy, but there is no such thing, especially on film, as an actor’s performance being entirely their own. There are costume people and other artists collaborating with them to create this character. The way the DP shoots you, the way the editor crafts it, that creates the final character.
	
		Your work on Rocky continued after filming, including helping the animators at Framestore. What did that involve?	

	After we wrapped, I got to see a cut and Phil and Chris asked, “Do you have any thoughts?” I said, “Well, I do. Are you sure?” I sent about seven or eight pages of notes about who Rocky is and how he moves, so the animators had more information and Framestore implemented that.

	When you’re getting a puppet on camera, you’re focused on the frame. But if they need to go back later and add a CG counterpart, what are they basing it off of? So I gave them hours and hours of me and my team with a smaller puppet covered in dots, playing full scenes without any breaks. It was a chance to throw in every good idea or any bad idea I had left that we wouldn’t have been able to shoot on the day.

	My team and I had worked out little bits of funny business. There’s a moment when Rocky has an epiphany and runs from one place to the other, and he falls ass over teakettle down this ramp. That was something we did on the reference table. When he sits on the beach at the end, his little legs wrap around him like a cinnamon bun. One of my puppeteers said, “It’s so cute. I’m desperate to find a way to put this in there.” I went, “Yes, this is it.” And they did it.
	
		SAG-AFTRA recognizes puppeteers as performers. What needs to change in the rest of the industry?	

	It’s one of the few unions ever that recognizes puppetry as performance. Theatrically, there’s actually no puppet representation, union-wise. Most of the time, puppeteers are considered crew and that means a variety of other things.
	

	Generally, when there’s on-set puppetry in a Star Wars movie or some big-budget genre thing, it’s been storyboarded within an inch of its life. The puppeteer is brought in: Here’s page five of scene six, he takes three steps and he turns. OK, that’s lunch. It’s much more technical. Phil and Chris and Ryan and all the producers were never interested in that. Working with Phil and Chris was such a, I’m trying not to curse, a friggin’ gift. It felt like being in a writers’ room, a fluid pitch meeting.

	I don’t know if credit is the point, but I do think acknowledging the effort, acknowledging that C-3PO was actually Anthony Daniels, there’s something to that. The goal of all of this is to create a character that you completely believe, so you don’t think about the other things. But from an industry standpoint, there’s going to be more genre storytelling, more characters we currently cannot imagine. How do we keep having these conversations? I have to keep giving flowers to Amazon MGM because they said this was such an unusual way of working, so why don’t we talk about it?
	
		How did Andy Serkis and his work as Gollum influence your approach to Rocky?	

	He was such a touchstone for how we approached Rocky. I was of the age where I ate up all those “Lord of the Rings” docs and special features. There’s probably a two-hour doc just about Gollum. I logged it away years ago. He walked so I could run. I am standing on the shoulders of many giants. I did not invent anything. But sometimes it’s a huge gift that someone else came before you, and you can point at something and go, “Like this.”
	
		What has the response been like to the conversation around your Oscar eligibility?	

	It’s overwhelming. I can’t process any of it. Who knows if any of this conversation leads to more? I don’t even want to say awareness. It’s not like a disease. Get tested for rocks. But this art form has always been there. It’s always going to be there. Obviously, the goal is to create a character that you get lost in, but I think there’s value in talking about the folks that made that.
	
		You’ve said that Rocky is the result of a collaborative art form. What do you hope audiences take away from that?	

	It’s a collaborative art form. There’s no version of it that happens by one person. Many singular people are on the poster at the end of the day, but that’s why the credits are so long. Every single one of those people bled and sweat and cried and probably got a divorce while they were making this thing.
	

	10 QUESTIONS WITH JAMES ORTIZ
	
		Something you loved as a kid that you can’t believe you were into?	

	As a kid, I was such a fan of “Batman Forever.” I was so nuts about Jim Carrey in that movie. It’s a great film, but there’s also a longer conversation there about the queer identity that I discovered in myself from that film, which is not rapid fire.
	
		Go-to karaoke or sing-in-the-shower song?	

	Oh, my God. Easy. I always run toward “Un-Break My Heart” by Toni Braxton, and occasionally, if we’re feeling frisky, I might do “Orange Colored Sky” by Natalie Cole.
	
		Give me an alternate title for “Project Hail Mary.”	

	“This Rock and This Man: What an Adventure!” It’s wordy, but I think it gets us there.
	
		What’s your secret talent?	

	I can clap with one hand. That’s going to sound disgusting, I know. It’s pretty terrifying.
	
		Favorite ice cream flavor?	

	It’s a childhood thing. Blue Bell is a Texas ice cream brand, and in the ’90s, they had a different formula for cookies and cream. It’s changed now, and I don’t like it, but the original, I really, really loved.
	
		The one item you couldn’t live without?	

	Probably my Apple Pencil, because I’m drawing all the time.
	
		What TV show or film in all of history do you wish you were a cast member of?	

	God, am I only going to talk about Batman? “Batman: The Animated Series.” It’s a show I still go back to all the time.
	
		Fictional character you most relate to or admire?	

	Honestly, the only thing that came to mind is Rocky.
	
		Your best piece of advice, either given or received?	

	Calm down. Take a fucking breath.
	

	Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television. Each episode, “Awards Circuit” features interviews with top film and TV talent and creatives, discussions and debates about awards races and industry headlines and much more. Subscribe via Apple Podcasts, Stitcher, Spotify or anywhere you download podcasts.

title: ‘Michael’ Won’t Be Submitted for BAFTA Awards as Filmmakers Pass on Billion-Dollar Biopic’s Entry (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
The highest-grossing biopic ever made is sitting out one of the biggest stops on the road to the Oscars.

	“Michael,” Antoine Fuqua’s billion-dolla
body:
The highest-grossing biopic ever made is sitting out one of the biggest stops on the road to the Oscars.

	“Michael,” Antoine Fuqua’s billion-dollar portrait of the King of Pop, will not be submitted for the 2027 EE BAFTA Film Awards, Variety has learned exclusively. That takes actors like Jaafar Jackson and Colman Domingo, along with the film’s entire craft team, out of the running before longlist voting begins.


	According to sources with direct knowledge, producer Graham King, Fuqua and various stakeholders made the call after consulting with Lionsgate, international distributor Universal Pictures and the film’s other partners. The sources cite “multiple factors” behind the decision but declined to say what they are.
	

	Representatives for Lionsgate, Universal Pictures and GK Films declined to comment.

	Sources tell Variety that Lionsgate and Universal supports the filmmakers’ decision.

	Earlier this month, the organization sent film voting members its Recommended Viewing Groups for the 2027 awards, which divides every entered film into 15 groups. Each member is randomly assigned one. The British Academy encourages voters to watch as many entries as they can but asks those short on time to prioritize their assigned group and the films in their specialist craft category. “Michael” isn’t in any of them.

	BAFTA’s Stage Two entry and deadline passed Nov. 19. A draft list of entered films goes out to entrants and members Nov. 26. The final list will be published on Dec. 4, the same morning Round One voting opens to set the longlists.
	

	Among the films that entered are “The Odyssey,” “Artificial,” “Behemoth!,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Wuthering Heights” and “The Social Reckoning.” The year’s other box office heavyweights, “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” are also in the mix, along with two music documentaries, “Epic: Elvis Presley in Concert” and “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.”

	It’s an unusual move for a film that has spent the fall building an awards case.

	The 80th BAFTA Film Awards reclaim its traditional spot ahead of the Academy this season. Last year, the British Academy announced nominations five days after the Oscars did, breaking a pattern that had held since 2001. This time, longlists arrive Jan. 7 and nominations Jan. 19, two days before the Academy unveils its own on Jan. 21. The London ceremony follows Feb. 21, three weeks ahead of the March 14 Oscars at the Dolby Theatre. For voters on both sides of the Atlantic, the BAFTA ballot is the first real read on the Oscar race, especially given the Academy’s large international voting bloc.

	It’s also a departure from producer King’s own playbook. “Bohemian Rhapsody,” his last music biopic, won Rami Malek the BAFTA for leading actor on the way to four Oscars, which he repeated.

	King has criticized the British Academy before. After February’s ceremony, Tourette’s syndrome campaigner John Davidson involuntarily shouted the N-word while “Sinners” stars Michael B. Jordan and Delroy Lindo presented the night’s first award, and the BBC aired the slur despite a two-hour tape delay. Both organizations apologized.

	“For years, BAFTA and the BBC have repeatedly displayed cultural insensitivity and tone deafness,” King said at the time in a statement posted to his GK Films’ Instagram account. “Their inability to take accountability for their actions or inactions is reckless and unacceptable.”

	The sources did not say whether the episode factored into this year’s decision.

	The news also comes after the Golden Globes rejected the studio’s bid to place “Michael” in the comedy or musical categories, a submission that came with a letter from Fuqua, pushing the film into the more crowded drama race. An FYC screening at the DGA reportedly drew a standing ovation.
	

	At the Gotham Awards on Nov. 30, Fuqua, King, Jaafar Jackson, Colman Domingo and Nia Long will accept the Musical Tribute Award.

	The commercial case was settled months ago, with a sequel currently in development.

	“Michael” opened in April to $97 million domestically and $217 million worldwide, a record debut for a music biopic. In July, it became the first biopic to cross $1 billion globally. It’s Lionsgate’s biggest release ever, topping the $865 million of “The Hunger Games: Catching Fire” and the studio says it’s the first film from an independent distributor to reach the milestone.

	The critics’ reception was much harsher than audiences’. The film currently holds a 38% score on Rotten Tomatoes. However, viewers have consistently singled out Jaafar Jackson’s star-making turn as his uncle; audiences gave it an A- CinemaScore.

	Written by John Logan, “Michael” traces Jackson’s rise from the Jackson 5 in the 1960s through the Bad World Tour in the late 1980s, closing before the first allegations of misconduct became public in 1993. Jaafar Jackson leads a cast that includes Domingo as Joseph Jackson, Long as Katherine Jackson, Miles Teller as attorney John Branca and Mike Myers as record executive Walter Yetnikoff.

	Skipping BAFTA doesn’t affect the film’s Oscar eligibility, and the Globes, Critics Choice Awards and guild circuits remain in play. But it gives up one of the season’s biggest televised platforms, along with one of the few chances for a breakout performance to reach an international voting body before Oscar nominations voting opens.

	Whether the decision ultimately costs “Michael” a trip to the Oscars remains to be seen.

body:
'Yes, Dear' Star Anthony Clark
                          Death Linked to Sepsis, Flu & Alcoholism
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Anthony Clark's official cause of death has been revealed ... and the "Yes, Dear" star's death certificate sheds new light on the health complications that claimed his life.
      
    
              The comedian died from septic shock on November 10 at age 63, according to a death certificate obtained by People.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The document also lists influenza A and chronic alcoholism as underlying conditions ... with acute kidney failure identified as a significant contributing factor.
      

              As TMZ previously reported ... Deadline initially attributed Clark's death to complications from pneumonia and the flu.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
              Clark's former "Yes, Dear" costar Mike O'Malley announced his passing on November 11, remembering his longtime friend as a hilarious comedian who could always get a laugh.
      
    
              O'Malley revealed the two had spoken on the phone just three weeks before Clark's death ... saying the conversation had them laughing once again.
      
    
              Clark was best known for playing Greg Warner on the CBS sitcom, which ran for six seasons from 2000 to 2006. He also starred in "Boston Common" and hosted the fourth season of "Last Comic Standing."

Actress Kimmarie Johnson
                          Cause of Death Revealed
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Kimmarie Johnson died from cardiac arrest ... though it appears cancer played a role as well.
      
    
              People obtained Kimmarie's death certificate ... and the outlet reports that cardiopulmonary arrest is listed as her primary cause of death.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              However, the outlet also notes an underlying cause of death is a metastatic granulosa cell ovarian tumor with peritoneal carcinomatosis.
      
    
              Basically, Kimmarie had a cancerous tumor ... and the cancer spread to the peritoneum -- a thin membrane lining the abdominal and pelvic cavities.
      

              We broke the story about Kimmarie's death ... revealing she'd died from some sort of heart issue earlier this month after she was rushed to the hospital. However, this is the first we're hearing about the cancer she was also dealing with.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              During her career, Kimmarie appeared in "Beverly Hills, 90210," "V.I.P.," and as a "Jumpsuit Chick" in "Dude, Where's My Car?"
      
    
              She was just 50 years old.
